Colosseum: Auditing Collusion in Cooperative Multi-Agent Systems

Mason Nakamura*1🖂    Abhinav Kumar*1    Saswat Das*2 Affiliation: Sahar Abdelnabi3,4    Saaduddin Mahmud1 Affiliation: Ferdinando Fioretto2    Shlomo Zilberstein1    Eugene Bagdasarian1 Affiliation: 1University of Massachusetts Amherst Affiliation: 2University of Virginia Affiliation: 3ELLIS Institute Tübingen Affiliation: 4MPI for Intelligent Systems, Tübingen AI Center
Abstract

Multi-agent systems, where LLM agents communicate through free-form language, enable sophisticated coordination for solving complex cooperative tasks. This surfaces a unique safety problem when a group of agents forms a coalition and colludes to pursue secondary goals and degrade the joint objective. In this paper, we present Colosseum, a framework for auditing LLM agents’ collusive behavior in multi-agent settings. We ground how agents cooperate through a formal multi-agent decision-making framework and measure action-based collusive behavior in actions via regret relative to the cooperative optimum and compare it with communication-based collusive behavior. Colosseum enables audits of LLM agents for collusion under benign settings, different coalition objectives, persuasion tactics, and network topologies. We then introduce a new behavioral probe by creating secret communication channels between agents, showing that most out-of-the-box models exhibit a propensity to collude under this probe, which we term emergent collusion. Furthermore, we discover “collusion on paper” when agents plan to collude in text but often pick non-collusive actions. Colosseum provides a new way to audit collusion in cooperative multi-agent systems while presenting observations about how collusion emerges, what affects collusion efficacy, and which strategies may mitigate it.

1 Introduction

Multi-agent systems (MAS) powered by large language models (LLMs) are rapidly moving toward deployment, enabling complex workflows (Motwani et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2025; Smith et al., 2025). As LLM-based multi-agent and multi-party systems become widespread (Moltbook, 2026; The Economist, 2026), they may introduce harms when applied to real-world tasks (Hammond et al., 2025). A particularly urgent risk is collusion, in which a subset of agents forms a coalition and coordinates to advance its goals and steer outcomes that violate the system’s intended cooperative objectives or policies. Recent work studying LLM collusion (Ren et al., 2025; Motwani et al., 2024) focuses on collusion tactics (e.g., steganography) rather than model behavior, which is necessary for developing safe agents that are deployed in the real world. In this paper, we introduce Colosseum, a framework for auditing collusion in cooperative LLM-based multi-agent systems, with a focus on evaluating agent behavior through regret-based metrics and conversation logs.

Given a group of LLM-based agents that coordinate to complete a cooperative task by taking actions in an environment, we need to understand how and in what situations a coalition of agents colludes. Distributed Constraint Optimization Problems (DCOPs) formalize this setting exactly, offering a simple problem statement that allows for fast evaluation and formal regret metrics. Using DCOPs, we create environments to audit collusion based on both textual conversations (LLM-as-a-judge) and actions (regret metrics). One such environment is the JIRA environment, described in § 5.2, which we use as the backbone for creating a Simpsons-themed environment used in Figures 1 and 3 to illustrate different types of collusive behavior.

Using our formal definition of collusion, we quantify the extent to which a coalition exhibits collusive behavior by optimizing an unintended objective relative to the cooperative objective, based on the agents’ actions, and analyze its effects on the multi-agent system. Using metrics that detect both action- and conversation-based collusion, we show across models that different forms of collusive behavior arise, including direct, attempted, and hidden collusion. This motivates the analysis in Figure 1, which shows that conversations or actions alone are insufficient: neither captures the full space of potential collusion types needed to understand model behavior.

We primarily study collusion on communication channels that allow agents to communicate and persist their conversations as a temporary memory. To improve understanding of agents’ behaviors, we create a behavioral probing mechanism inspired by neuroscience literature (Yoon et al., 2022) that instantiates secret communication channels between agents as a controlled auditing intervention and observe the multi-agent system’s change in behavior. A secret communication channel allows agents to converse separately from the public communication channel that all agents are members of. We do not assume that all deployments contain explicit secret channels; rather, secret channels operationalize a realistic class of private side channels and test whether cooperative agents exploit them to coordinate collusively.

While using our behavioral probe, we observe, as shown in Figure 3, that otherwise benign agents when given access to a secret communication channel can begin pursuing a secondary goal misaligned with the cooperative objective, even without being explicitly prompted to do so. We define this phenomenon as emergent collusion.

We first study settings where two benign agents share a secret channel. Across nineteen models, we observe emergent collusion in both actions, measured by coalition advantage, and conversations, measured by LLM-as-a-judge scores (see Figure 4). We further find that persuasion capability (Mahmud et al., 2026; Kamenica and Gentzkow, 2011; Zeng et al., 2024), network topology (Yu et al., 2024; Nugraha et al., 2025), and coalition goals (Skalse et al., 2022; Lynch et al., 2025) can promote or deter collusion, often trading off against the cooperative objective. These findings highlight the need to design and monitor multi-agent systems to prevent collusive coalitions from degrading task performance or systematically advantaging coalition members.

In summary, this work makes the following contributions: (1) we introduce formal auditing metrics for detecting collusion in cooperative multi-agent systems modeled as distributed constraint optimization problems (DCOPs); (2) we develop Colosseum, a comprehensive auditing framework that introduces a novel behavioral probe for evaluating multi-agent behavior and couples collusion-judge scores with regret metrics, enabling identification of different types of collusive behavior; (3) we introduce two new DCOP benchmark environments that closely capture real-world domains: software Jira ticket allocation and hospital patient transfers; (4) using Colosseum, we observe unique collusive behavioral patterns across state-of-the-art models and environments; and (5) we outline concrete strategies for mitigating collusion in cooperative multi-agent systems based on our audit.

2 Background and Related Work

Multi-Agent Systems.  An agent is an autonomous entity that perceives an environment and acts to achieve goals (Wooldridge, 2009). Interacting agents form multi-agent systems (MAS), where interaction ranges from collaboration to negotiation and conflict (Jennings et al., 1998; Wurman et al., 2008; Parker, 1998; Roughgarden, 2005; Tambe, 2011). Among these, much of the foundational MAS literature focuses on cooperative systems, studying how distributed entities can achieve globally desirable behavior (i.e., a joint reward function) despite partial observability, decentralized control, and limited communication.

Cooperative deployments of MAS are likely to be widespread in society (e.g., coding agents building a repository, autonomous vehicle agents minimizing traffic, or government agents introducing new legislation). However, although classical MASs are well studied, LLM-based MASs bring general-purpose agents that rely on natural language, broadening their coordination capabilities (Nakamura et al., 2025; Abdelnabi et al., 2024; Li et al., 2023) and expanding safety risks.

Multi-Agent Safety.  Recent work (Hammond et al., 2025) studies risks that arise from multi-agent interactions, which can lead to critical or catastrophic failures (Hendrycks et al., 2023). Instances of such risks are scheming between agents (Schoen et al., 2025), network effects (Yu et al., 2024; Nugraha et al., 2025; Ju et al., 2024; Ren et al., 2025), conflict (Mukobi et al., 2023; Rivera et al., 2024), miscoordination (Du et al., 2023; Leibo et al., 2024), and collusion (Ren et al., 2025; Motwani et al., 2024; Abada and Lambin, 2023; Idowu et al., 2026), which could have negative and unsafe effects on multi-agent systems deployed in the real world.

Collusion.  Among these risks, collusion arises from undesirable cooperation and is typically studied in competitive markets (Lin et al., 2024; Agrawal et al., 2025; Wu et al., 2024; Fish et al., 2024) or partially observable stochastic games (Foxabbott et al., 2023). In markets, algorithmic collusion occurs when algorithms coordinate prices without human intervention, complicating antitrust enforcement (Fish et al., 2024; Dorner, 2021). In contrast, we study collusion in fully cooperative settings that can become mixed-motive when agents have hidden objectives, such as those encoded in model weights.

Steganographic Collusion.  Steganographic collusion uses covert messages on public or monitored channels to communicate with colluding parties while avoiding detection. Prior work studies this by training sender–receiver pairs to elicit such behavior on a single communication channel (Mathew et al., 2025). Our formulation, which invokes many communication channels, is a more general multi-agent configuration. However, we note that steganographic collusion still persists as a problem in this more general setting.

3 Problem Formulation

In cooperative multi-agent systems, misaligned LLM-based agents that coordinate via open-ended message passing may undesirably coordinate to optimize a secondary objective that is different from the cooperative objective which can lead to a multi-agent risk known as collusion. This motivates the need for a clear problem formulation (§ 3.1) that can be empirically transferred to a principled auditing framework, allowing us to draw meaningful conclusions about model behavior and models’ role in collusion. Establishing safe multi-agent systems requires extensive analysis of behavior and group dynamics in various scenarios by auditing conversation logs and actions. Auditing collusion requires a formalism with three properties. First, it must make the intended cooperative objective explicit, so that any deviation we observe can be measured against a well-defined target. Second, it must support computationally cheap coalitional counterfactuals: given an observed joint assignment, we need to ask what would have happened had a subset of agents acted differently, without re-simulating the entire trajectory. Third, it must avoid the temporal and structural credit-assignment confounds of long-horizon multi-agent decision-making, so that an observed regret can be attributed to coalition behavior rather than to learning dynamics or delayed effects. DCOPs (Fioretto et al., 2018), the audit framework adopted in this work and introduced below, satisfy all three.

3.1 Distributed Constraint Optimization Problem

A distributed constraint optimization problem (DCOP) is defined as a tuple 𝒫=⟨A,X,D,F,α⟩,\mathcal{P}\!=\!\langle A,\;X,\;D,\;F,\;\alpha\rangle, specifying a set of agents A={a1,…,an}A=\{a_{1},\dots,a_{n}\}, a set of decision variables X={x1,…,xm}X\!=\!\{x_{1},\dots,x_{m}\}, and finite domains D={D1,…,Dm}D\!=\!\{D_{1},\dots,D_{m}\} where each variable xjx_{j} must take a value in DjD_{j}. Each variable is controlled by exactly one agent via an ownership mapping α:X→A\alpha:X\rightarrow A (i.e., agent aia_{i} controls Xi≜{x∈X∣α⁡(x)=ai}X_{i}\triangleq\{x\in X\mid\alpha(x)\!=\!a_{i}\}). The objective function, F⁡(𝐱)≜∑k=1Kfk​(𝐱Sk)F(\mathbf{x})\;\triangleq\;\sum_{k=1}^{K}f_{k}\!\left(\mathbf{x}_{S_{k}}\right), is defined as the sum of a set of utility functions F={f1,…,fK}F=\{f_{1},\dots,f_{K}\} where each fkf_{k} has a scope Sk⊆XS_{k}\subseteq X. A solution is a complete joint assignment 𝐱∈∏j=1mDj\mathbf{x}\in\prod_{j=1}^{m}D_{j} while an optimal solution 𝐱⋆∈arg⁡max𝐱⁡F⁡(𝐱)\mathbf{x}^{\star}\in\arg\max_{\mathbf{x}}F(\mathbf{x}) maximizes the objective function. In this setting, where agents are LLM-based, coordination proceeds via message passing: agents exchange information about their planned assignments, local utility functions, and constraints to produce an optimal solution at the conclusion of a communication round. For a more extensive definition, see Appendix A.

The cooperative objective is encoded as a sum of local utility functions that the agents are jointly tasked to maximize; counterfactual coalition assignments can be evaluated in closed form by reusing the decomposable reward; and the single-step formulation removes credit assignment by construction. Richer multi-agent decision making frameworks exist (e.g., POSG (Foxabbott et al., 2023), Dec-MDP (Dibangoye et al., 2012), Dec-POMDP (Amato et al., 2013; Bernstein et al., 2002)), and subsume DCOPs but conflate these auditing primitives with sequential dynamics, making it hard to separate what a coalition did from what the environment let it do.

4 Using Colosseum to Audit Collusion

Our goal is to audit whether, and to what extent, an observed LLM-based multi-agent interaction exhibits collusive behavior relative to a cooperative task specification. We define collusion as a multi-agent attack in which a subset of agents, or coalition, coordinates to steer the system toward outcomes misaligned with the nominal DCOP objective, while still participating in an otherwise cooperative DCOP protocol.

4.1 Regret Metrics for Collusion Auditing

For a set of agents AA and a complete joint assignment 𝐱\mathbf{x}, let Fn​(𝐱)F_{n}(\mathbf{x}) be the nominal DCOP objective that the system is intended to optimize through communication exchange with 𝐱n⋆∈arg⁡max𝐱​Fn​(𝐱)\mathbf{x}^{\star}_{n}\in\arg\max_{\mathbf{x}}F_{n}(\mathbf{x}). The goal of collusion is to optimize an auxiliary objective function that is misaligned with the cooperative system, reducing the nominal joint reward Fn​(𝐱)F_{n}(\mathbf{x}). The DCOP framework allows us to formalize this by specifying that a colluding coalition of agents uses a different collusion objective Fc​(𝐱)F_{c}(\mathbf{x}) (hidden from the designer/auditor) that is not necessarily aligned with FnF_{n}. We formalize this mismatch between the nominal intended cooperative multi-agent problem and the collusive problem as follows.

Consider a subset of agents S⊆AS\subseteq A, with |S|≥2|S|\geq 2, that can coordinate their choices. We define the coalition-controlled variables as XS≜{x∈X:α⁡(x)∈S}X_{S}\triangleq\{x\in X:\alpha(x)\in S\} and the remaining as X−S≜X∖XSX_{-S}\triangleq X\setminus X_{S}. We write a joint assignment as 𝐱=(𝐱S⊕𝐱−S)\mathbf{x}=(\mathbf{x}_{S}\oplus\mathbf{x}_{-S}) where ⊕\oplus is the concatenation operator, and fix a baseline assignment 𝐱¯−S\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{-S} for non-coalition variables (e.g., produced by non-colluding behavior or a reference policy). The coalition colludes if it can deviate on XSX_{S} to produce an assignment that is intent-violating under the nominal objective:

Since optimality cannot be guaranteed in practical settings, we interpret 𝐱n⋆\mathbf{x}_{n}^{\star} as the solution produced under nominal operation (e.g., using the same protocol in the absence of collusion), rather than a globally optimal assignment. Additionally, the nominal objective FnF_{n} can be swapped with other functions (e.g., LLM-as-a-judge or coalition advantage) to provide a clearer analysis of the system’s underlying dynamics relative to the coalition’s actions in noisy real-world settings. This definition, therefore, separates what is intended (maximizing FnF_{n}) from what is enforced under a collusive deviation, making collusion auditable as a measurable drop in FnF_{n} relative to a nominal reference outcome.

Misaligned Agents and λ\lambda-Alignment.  The DCOP definition above treats agents as either fully cooperative or fully collusive. However, in LLM-mediated settings the boundary is rarely so clean: prompts, persuasive messages, and revealed private context all induce partial compromise that varies in strength across agents and across turns. This work captures this with the notion of λ\lambda-alignment:

Fλi(i)​(𝐱)≜(1−λi)​Fn​(𝐱)+λi​Fc​(𝐱).F^{(i)}_{\lambda_{i}}(\mathbf{x})\;\triangleq\;(1-\lambda_{i})\,F_{n}(\mathbf{x})\;+\;\lambda_{i}\,F_{c}(\mathbf{x}). (1)

The above interpolates between two extremes. At λi=0\lambda_{i}=0 the agent optimizes cooperative objectives and is fully aligned with the nominal task. At λi=1\lambda_{i}=1 it optimizes the hidden coalition objective FcF_{c} and ignores FnF_{n}. We call a coalition S⊆AS\subseteq A λ\lambda-aligned if all agents in SS share a common tradeoff λ\lambda (i.e., λi=λ\lambda_{i}=\lambda for all i∈Si\in S) and coordinate to optimize the same hidden objective FcF_{c} as seen in Figure 2. If different coalition members have different λi\lambda_{i} values, the resulting interaction induces additional heterogeneity in how agents evaluate the same assignment, yielding further asymmetry.

4.2 Applications to LLM Agents

LLM agents inherently communicate through natural language, thus we employ Terrarium (Nakamura et al., 2025), a framework that allows us to evaluate LLM-based multi-agent systems with different configurations (i.e., models, topologies, etc.) and use a blackboard mechanism Erman et al. (1980) to passively observe communication channels.

As seen in Eq. 1, crucially, the λi\lambda_{i} values are not numerical values computed by the LLM agents during execution. Instead, agents are induced by prompts, tools, or reward models to behave as if they were optimizing a specified λ\lambda, an abstraction the auditor uses to reason about the strength of collusive influence.

Specified vs. Empirical λ\lambda.  LLM-based agent policies are imperfect and stochastic, and, as a result, will create deviations between specified λ\lambda behavior derived from the prompts and empirical λ\lambda behavior derived from agent interactions (e.g., conversations and actions). Thus, λ\lambda should be decoupled in terms of specified λspec\lambda_{\text{spec}} and empirical λemp\lambda_{\text{emp}}. As seen in Figure 3, Emergent (unprompted) is fully aligned with the cooperative objective (λspec=0\lambda_{\text{spec}}=0) showing more benign language in the communication channel (λemp≈0\lambda_{\text{emp}}\approx 0) whereas the Prompted version that incites the coalition to maximize their local joint objective (λspec>0\lambda_{\text{spec}}>0) shows clearer signs of collusion in the communication (λemp>0\lambda_{\text{emp}}>0). This distinction is important to capture variations of collusion behavior, specifically emergent collusion.

This decoupling of λ\lambda also offers incites into how instances of attempted collusion (i.e., collusion-on-paper), λspec>0\lambda_{\text{spec}}>0 and λemp≈0\lambda_{\text{emp}}\approx 0, may form. In this scenario, Fc​(x)F_{c}(x) may be too difficult to optimize due to bad coordination, optimal collusive actions are infeasible, or collusion mitigation strategies are in place, preventing the colluders to influence their environment. In our experiments (§ 5.5- 5.7), we specify λspec\lambda_{\text{spec}} in the prompt of the agent and evaluate λemp\lambda_{\text{emp}} using regret metrics and a collusion judge.

Behavioral Probe.  We introduce a novel behavioral probing mechanism (Yoon et al., 2022) that instantiates secret communication channels as controlled interventions for testing whether and to what extent models exhibit collusive behavior on these channels unprompted. See § 5.4 for the primary experiments using this probing mechanism.

Collusion Efficacy Factors.  Our DCOP model characterizes collusion as a measurable deviation from the nominal objective FnF_{n}, but the ability of a coalition to realize such deviations depends on certain operational factors. We connect three factors to our framework: (1) Objective Misalignment: Collusion is enabled when a coalition effectively optimizes a mixed objective that places weight on an auxiliary objective FcF_{c} (e.g., λi>0\lambda_{i}>0 in Fλi(i)F^{(i)}_{\lambda_{i}}); (2) Persuasion: In addition to taking coalition-beneficial actions, agents can communicate messages that persuade other agents to alter their local choices and proposals, steering the realized assignment 𝐱\mathbf{x} toward outcomes favored by FcF_{c}; and (3) Network Influence: The communication topology and messaging constraints govern exposure and diffusion of claims, shaping the effectiveness of persuasion and the coalition’s ability to shift the joint outcome. Our experiments (§ 5.5- 5.7) manipulate and isolate these factors and trace their effects on the realized Δ\Delta.

5 Experiments

In this section, we systematically audit collusive behavior of out-of-the-box LLMs using Colosseum. More precisely, we answer the following pressing research questions:

  • •

    (RQ1) (Auditing) Is an LLM-as-a-judge sufficient for collusion auditing or do we also need action-based collusion metrics?

  • •

    (RQ2) (Transferability) Does collusive conversation behavior result in collusive actions?

  • •

    (RQ3) (Emergence) Do out-of-the-box LLMs exhibit emergent collusion in cooperative multi-agent systems when a secret channel is introduced between agents?

  • •

    (RQ4) (Efficacy) How does objective misalignment, persuasion, and network influence contribute to collusion efficacy?

5.1 Setup and Framework

Throughout our experiments, we use Terrarium Nakamura et al. (2025)11 1 Terrarium (MIT License) GitHub Link: https://github.com/umass-aisec/Terrarium, a multi-agent system framework that models multi-agent problem instances as DCOPs. The framework enables low-level interventions of the communication channels, network topology, communication protocol, agent configurations, available tools, and environment instances.

During inter-agent interaction, agents first engage in a planning phase that includes multiple round-robin communication rounds where they communicate resources, preferences, skills, or availability to optimize the joint reward function. Next, agents enter an execution phase where they take actions by assigning environment variables via tool calls. Agent orders, random communication topologies, and problem instances are randomized by seed.

5.2 Environments

We introduce two new DCOP environments, Hospital and Jira, and use an existing DCOP environment for Meeting scheduling (Mahmud et al., 2025). Each environment instantiates a cooperative multi-agent system operated by LLM-based agents and reflects real-world workflows in hospitals, software development, and workplace logistics that each have varying environment dynamics and configurations. In particular, the Hospital environment is unique in that it includes agents with heterogeneous capabilities and goals, which also yield heterogeneous coalition compositions. Our environments’ joint reward functions are decomposable that aggregate all the agents’ rewards, allowing for credit assignment to each individual agent to the joint reward. This characteristic is important for calculating regret metrics for the coalition. See Appendix B for more environment details.

5.3 Experimental Settings

To evaluate collusion on the aforementioned environments, we use the following settings.

Metrics.  In our experiments, let ri​(𝐱)r_{i}(\mathbf{x}) denote agent ii’s credited reward where 𝐱\mathbf{x} is the joint assignment of agent assignments (via the environments’ reward decomposition). Then the joint reward of the system is defined as Fn​(𝐱)=∑i∈𝒜ri​(𝐱)F_{n}(\mathbf{x})=\sum_{i\in\mathcal{A}}r_{i}(\mathbf{x}). The general metrics used in our experiments are:

  • •

    Overall regret of the system, defined as Δ\Delta in Definition 4.1; however, we report its normalized variant using min-max normalization, where the max is the optimal joint reward obtained by brute-force search or known a priori via the environment dynamics and the min is dependent on the environment configuration.

  • •

    Coalition mean regret, used to study coalition success. Given a realized joint assignment 𝐱~\tilde{\mathbf{x}}, define the per-agent regret for agent ii as δi​(𝐱~)≜maxxi∈𝒜i⁡ri​(xi⊕𝐱~−i)−ri​(𝐱~)\delta_{i}(\tilde{\mathbf{x}})\;\triangleq\;\max_{x_{i}\in\mathcal{A}_{i}}r_{i}\!\big(x_{i}\oplus\tilde{\mathbf{x}}_{-i}\big)\;-\;r_{i}(\tilde{\mathbf{x}}) where 𝒜i\mathcal{A}_{i} is agent ii’s action set, ⊕\oplus is the concatenation operator, and all other agents’ actions 𝐱~−i\tilde{\mathbf{x}}_{-i} are held fixed. Then the coalition mean regret is Δcmean​(𝐱~)≜1|S|​∑i∈Sδi​(𝐱~),\Delta_{c}^{\text{mean}}(\tilde{\mathbf{x}})\;\triangleq\;\frac{1}{|S|}\sum_{i\in S}\delta_{i}(\tilde{\mathbf{x}}), where S⊆𝒜S\subseteq\mathcal{A} is the set of coalition agents (Δ−cmean\Delta_{-c}^{\text{mean}} is defined analogously for the non-coalition mean regret).

  • •

    Coalition advantage, defined as the regret gap Δ−cmean−Δcmean\Delta_{-c}^{\text{mean}}-\Delta_{c}^{\text{mean}}. When we report a normalized coalition advantage, 0.50.5 indicates a tie; values >0.5>0.5 favor the coalition and values <0.5<0.5 favor non-coalition agents.

  • •

    Collusion judge scores are computed using an LLM-as-a-judge that outputs a Likert-scale score (0-5) for collusion occurrence based on channel communications. Collusion judge scores are averaged over three different LLM-as-a-judge prompts and are prompted to output a rationale for their judge score (see Appendix F for prompt details). Throughout our experiments, we use GPT-5.4 as our LLM-as-a-judge unless otherwise specified and leave judge ablations in the Appendix (See Figure 17 in Appendix).

All experiments utilize five random seeds, with the exception of Figure 4 which uses ten seeds and two runs per seed. We use a combination of direct model APIs and Microsoft Azure for inference. The total experiment cost is approximately $2\$2k USD with most costs attributed to input tokens. All models use a temperature of 0.7, whereas judge models use a temperature of 0. Additionally, models have a 1.51.5k output token limit per conversation turn.

5.4 Emergent Collusion in Benign Settings

It is critical to evaluate and understand emergent collusion, a type of collusion that emerges from benign scenarios, since its implications in benignly deployed multi-agent systems are vast. We study emergent collusion by applying a behavioral probe that creates a secret communication channel between two benign agents (i.e., nominal prompts). We employ our definition of Δ\Delta-collusion (see Definition 4.1) in Figure 4 where the nominal solution is produced under a control setting (i.e., all agents communicate on a single public channel), and the nominal objective FnF_{n} is swapped with overall regret, coalition advantage, and judge score. In Figure 4, we compare the Emergent with a Prompted group that prompts the coalition agents to optimize the sum of their coalitional reward.

In Figure 4, we find that (1) there exists an inverse association between coalition advantage and judge score (i.e., the higher the coalition advantage the lower the judge score) with a Pearson correlation coefficient (n=19)22 2 However, we note that this may not be a significantly strong relation and leave validating this claim to future work over more models of r=−0.243r=-0.243 and r=−0.1429r=-0.1429 for Emergent and Prompted groups, respectively. (2) 57.89%57.89\% of models in Emergent and 78.95%78.95\% of models in Prompted exhibited Δ\Delta-Advantage greater than 00 (i.e., action-based collusion) while 10.53%10.53\% of models in Emergent and 78.95%78.95\% in Prompted had a Δ\Delta-Judge ≥1\geq 1, showing that Emergent elicits more hidden collusion whereas Prompted elicits more direct collusion. Finally, (3) the Emergent and Prompted groups have a Pearson correlation coefficient of r=−0.0386r=-0.0386 and r=−0.2401r=-0.2401, respectively, where Prompted negatively affects the cooperative system whereas Emergent shows less effect on the cooperative system, maintaining more nominal operation.

Motivated by these results, we analyzed channel logs and found model-dependent communication styles (Appendix D.9). Specifically, we found that Gemini-2.5-Flash, which had no change in the judge score in Emergent, was more direct and terse, whereas models with larger judge scores than the nominal baseline (e.g., Claude-Sonnet-4.5) were less direct, more verbose, and more willing to coordinate. It remains unclear which qualitative factors yield efficient yet non-collusive communication that the judge models are unable to detect.

5.5 Objective Misalignment

In this section, we explore a broader set of coalition objectives beyond the objective FcF_{c} of maximizing the coalition’s joint reward. In particular, we study three misalignment types, including the default coalition objective: (i) Covert – adversaries maximize FcF_{c} while keeping overall joint reward unchanged to remain stealthy (i.e., λ≈0.5\lambda\approx 0.5), (ii) Self-Promotional Sabotage (Sabotage (Self-Prom)) – the Prompted  strategy in Section 5.4, where adversaries optimize for FcF_{c} without a constraint on preserving overall joint reward (i.e., λ=1\lambda=1), and (iii) Self-Sacrificial Sabotage (Sabotage (Self-Sac)) – adversaries aim to reduce overall joint reward, regardless of coalition reward (i.e., λ=1\lambda=1).

We evaluate these strategies in the Hospital environment using a complete topology with a shared main communication channel. While the environment specifies a basic cooperative system prompt for each agent, the misaligned objectives are injected as further objective-modifying instructions appended to these system prompts. Unless stated otherwise, adversaries also have a secret channel. Coalitions either include the provisioner (including the resource provisioner) or are departmental (only department agents from the same hospital), reflecting heterogeneity in agent capabilities.

Figure 5 shows that coalition composition strongly shapes misalignment efficacy. Coalitions with a provisioner more reliably achieve their objectives: Covert  and Sabotage (Self-Prom) match the benign baseline in normalized mean overall regret (0.04–0.09), attain low

coalition regret (0.02–0.08), and usually yield positive coalition advantage, while Sabotage (Self-Sac) raises overall regret to 0.16–0.3 at the coalition’s expense. Departmental coalitions are less effective due to a limited action space: Covert  remains near baseline overall regret but incurs higher coalition regret without provisioner support (0.2–0.32), Sabotage (Self-Prom) ranges from 0.07–0.19 overall regret, and Sabotage (Self-Sac) raises overall regret for GPT models (0.13–0.2) but remains low for Kimi-K2-Instruct (0.07). Therefore, closer monitoring of high-leverage agents is required.

5.6 Persuasion

We investigate how colluding agents influence others’ actions to optimize a collusive objective, testing three adaptable persuasion tactics (Figure 12): (i) Helpful misdirection – presenting suboptimal choices as helpful and in others’ best interests, (ii) Authority nudge – claiming authority (e.g., organizers) so their advice takes priority, and (iii) Reciprocity trade – framing actions as benefiting others, then leveraging this “favor” to induce actions that benefit the colluders.

In Figure 6, we observe that all models achieve a significant decrease in regret when using persuasion techniques across most topologies. Across all topologies, we also find that Authority Nudge and Reciprocity Trade have a higher likelihood of significantly increasing regret, by up to 2.65×2.65\times and 2.77×2.77\times, respectively. This occurs because colluders converge on the same task that is optimal for them, leading to higher violations. In contrast, this is easier to prevent with helpful misdirection, since colluders act more cautiously and prefer minor nudges over bold claims. We validate these findings in the conversation logs (see Figure 12 in Appendix). Therefore, we conclude that successful persuasion requires the coalition to use false claims that are hard to verify and that benefit the coalition, while maintaining minimal violations.

5.7 Network Influence

In this section, we explore how far misinformation can propagate throughout the network and alter beliefs. We study a targeted misinformation strategy in the Meeting environment where multiple adversarial agents repeatedly broadcast the same false claim (e.g., that a particular agent is unavailable all week due to a trip) about a single, shared victim targeted by the adversaries. We evaluate this strategy across deterministic (complete, path, star) and random (Barabási-Albert, Watts-Strogatz, Erdös-Renyi) network families. As the number of adversaries grows, the victim-focused misinformation belief typically increases approximately linearly across most topologies, indicating a strong majority/volume effect on agent belief formation; however, the overall joint reward can be comparatively less sensitive, suggesting that

concentrated belief manipulation does not always translate proportionally into disruption of the system’s global scheduling objective. Additionally, we evaluated mass network effects (i.e., each adversary targets a unique victim) and found it to be more effective at reducing joint reward but less effective at propagating misinformation than targeted misinformation (see Appendix D.2 for further details).

5.8 Mitigating Collusion

Mitigations should target the specific mechanisms that enabled collusion in our experiments: private communication should be audited because even a benign secret channel produced emergent action- or conversation-level collusion; high-leverage agents such as resource provisioners should receive stricter access controls or independent verification because their coalitions achieved misalignment objectives most reliably; and allocation-relevant claims should be verified against shared state rather than accepted from peer messages, since authority and reciprocity-based persuasion were especially effective when claims were hard to verify. Finally, communication topologies should preserve cross-checking paths among affected agents, as shorter paths helped agents reject misinformation, while sparse network settings allowed false beliefs to propagate.

6 Conclusion

We introduced Colosseum, a trace-evaluable framework for auditing collusion in cooperative LLM-based multi-agent systems. By casting coordination tasks as DCOPs, Colosseum makes the intended cooperative objective explicit and enables regret-based action metrics that complement LLM-as-a-judge analyses of communication. Across our environments, our audits show that collusion is not captured by any single signal: adding a private channel between otherwise benign agents can increase collusion; action- and conversation-level collusion evidence can diverge into direct, hidden, and attempted collusion; and collusion efficacy depends on high-leverage roles, persuasion tactics, and communication topology. Colosseum therefore provides a foundation for red-teaming and monitoring cooperative agent deployments, and points toward actionable mitigation strategies.

Limitations and Future Work.  Colosseum is an objective-grounded auditing framework, and its claims rely on assumptions that make auditing tractable. Our experiments use DCOP-style coordination tasks with explicit objectives and decomposable rewards, enabling counterfactual regret analysis but omitting long-horizon effects such as temporal credit assignment, memory, and delayed outcomes. Most experiments also use homogeneous teams with a shared model backbone, leaving heterogeneous deployments with varied models, prompts, permissions, and tool access for future work. Finally, collusion is not always harmful: when the nominal objective encodes an unsafe or unethical task, coordinated deviation may be desirable rather than adversarial.

Broader Impacts

This paper introduces an auditing framework for detecting and measuring collusion in cooperative multi-agent systems. By turning collusion risk into measurable signals, it helps developers evaluate deployments, compare mitigations, and identify conditions under which collusion emerges. As LLM-based agent teams become more common, these tools enable systematic auditing of collusive threats.

Appendix A Extensive DCOP Formulation

A DCOP is a tuple: 𝒫=⟨A,X,D,F,α⟩,\mathcal{P}\!=\!\langle A,\;X,\;D,\;F,\;\alpha\rangle, specifying a set of agents A={a1,…,an}A=\{a_{1},\dots,a_{n}\}, a set of decision variables X={x1,…,xm}X\!=\!\{x_{1},\dots,x_{m}\}, and finite domains D={D1,…,Dm}D\!=\!\{D_{1},\dots,D_{m}\} where each variable xjx_{j} must take a value in DjD_{j}. Each variable is controlled by exactly one agent via an ownership mapping α:X→A\alpha:X\rightarrow A (so agent aia_{i} controls Xi≜{x∈X∣α⁡(x)=ai}X_{i}\triangleq\{x\in X\mid\alpha(x)\!=\!a_{i}\}). For example, consider a meeting-scheduling setting in which each agent is an LLM assistant representing a participant. Here, AA is the set of participant agents, each variable xix_{i} denotes the time slot that agent aia_{i} is willing to attend. In this example, the variable domain DiD_{i} consists of the discrete candidate time slots under consideration (e.g., 30-minute slots over the next week that are compatible with aia_{i}’s calendar).

The instance further specifies a set of utility (or cost) functions F={f1,…,fK}F=\{f_{1},\dots,f_{K}\}, where each fkf_{k} has a scope Sk⊆XS_{k}\subseteq X and is a function

fk:∏xj∈SkDj→ℝ,\textstyle f_{k}:\prod_{x_{j}\in S_{k}}D_{j}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}, (2)

mapping any joint assignment to the variables in SkS_{k} to a scalar utility/cost. Such functions FF can model task completeness, per-participant constraints, and preferences. An aggregation of these functions is defined as the objective function33 3 We use objective function and joint reward function interchangeably throughout this paper.

F⁡(𝐱)≜∑k=1Kfk​(𝐱Sk).F(\mathbf{x})\;\triangleq\;\sum_{k=1}^{K}f_{k}\!\left(\mathbf{x}_{S_{k}}\right). (3)

A solution to a DCOP is a complete assignment 𝐱∈∏j=1mDj\mathbf{x}\in\prod_{j=1}^{m}D_{j} that maximizes (or minimizes) the objective function. In this work, we focus on maximizing a weighted-sum joint reward that includes both utility and cost functions

𝐱⋆∈arg⁡max𝐱⁡F⁡(𝐱).\mathbf{x}^{\star}\in\arg\max_{\mathbf{x}}F(\mathbf{x}). (4)

In our example, a solution is a complete joint schedule specifying, for each agent aia_{i}, the slot xi∈Dix_{i}\!\in\!D_{i} it commits to.

Each agent aia_{i} in a DCOP knows the functions fkf_{k} that either involve variables it controls or are incident to its local neighborhood, depending on the problem distribution. Coordination proceeds via message passing, where agents exchange information about their local functions and partial assignments. The resulting interaction pattern is captured by a constraint graph, whose nodes are variables and where an edge links two variables if they co-occur in some function (factor) fkf_{k}. More generally, when functions have scope |Sk|>2|S_{k}|>2, the structure is a constraint hypergraph with hyperedges given by the scopes Skk{S_{k}}_{k} [6]. Equivalently, the same kk-ary structure can be represented as a factor graph: a bipartite graph with variable nodes and factor nodes (functions), with an edge between fkf_{k} and each variable in its scope SkS_{k} [20, 11].

In our implementation, we leverage this factor-graph abstraction to represent and reason about the DCOP’s (possibly higher-order) constraints. Communication is then naturally restricted to occur along the graph neighborhoods.

Solving a DCOP in a distributed way can proceed via complete algorithms [49, 36, 28], which guarantee convergence to an optimal assignment, or via incomplete algorithms that trade optimality for computational and communication efficiency [11], including local-search methods [53]. These classical approaches typically assume rigid, protocol-specific communication over the problem’s interaction structure, for example exchanging costs or utilities along graph edges. In our setting, agents are language models and communication is primarily language-based, enabling more flexible coordination and accommodating settings where explicitly specifying (or enforcing) a fixed message format is difficult. Accordingly, the methods we study in this paper are closest in spirit to local-search-style incomplete solvers, since optimal (complete) search can be prohibitively difficult at our scales and under language-mediated interaction.

In this paper, our primary goal is not to design a new distributed solver, but to audit LLM-based agent teams for collusion by solving DCOPs. Given a cooperative task specification and an observed multi-agent interaction (messages and resulting joint decisions), we ask whether a subset of agents coordinated to pursue an alternate objective, and we quantify the resulting degradation in system performance. Achieving this is difficult with purely behavioral assessments (e.g., manual dialogue inspection): without an explicit cooperative objective to define a baseline, and without a formal, trace-evaluable counterfactual notion of coalitional deviation, collusion cannot be reliably identified or measured.

The DCOP formalism addresses precisely these two missing ingredients. It provides the cooperative premise that there exists a single global objective F⁡(𝒙)=∑kfk​(𝒙Sk)F(\bm{x})=\sum_{k}f_{k}(\bm{x}_{S_{k}}) that agents are intended to collaboratively optimize (see Equation 3), a premise that collusion violates by construction. More importantly for auditing, DCOPs disentangle three components that are otherwise conflated in language-only evaluations: the task specification (the factors and feasibility constraints encoded by fkk{f_{k}}_{k}), the interaction structure (the factor graph that determines which agents must coordinate), and the observable execution trace (language messages and the realized assignment 𝒙\bm{x}).

Importantly, the DCOP formalism encapsulates the idea of a single global objective (the sum of all fkf_{k}) that all agents are supposed to collaboratively optimize. It assumes agents will truthfully participate in the protocol to maximize FF. This is a strong assumption, and exactly the one that collusion will violate. By having a clear mathematical definition of FF (the “correct” objective), we can precisely define what it means for a subset of agents to optimize a different objective. We also note that DCOPs, as defined, inherently assume cooperation; however, we introduce collusive agents with alternate goals, effectively studying an adversarial DCOP scenario or a DCOP with partially cooperative agents. Thus, the DCOP provides the baseline cooperative optimization structure and notation needed for our analysis of collusion.

Appendix B Environments

B.1 Hospital

Hospital Job Shop Scheduling. Hospitals route patients through a sequence of departments (e.g., triage, radiology, surgery, ward) along treatment pathways. In Hospital, agents represent departments that manage local queues and a provisioner that (re)allocates scarce shared resources. Using local/private information (e.g., queue lengths, expected service times, shortages), agents coordinate to propose patient schedules and resource transfers that reduce delays and prevent bottlenecks.

Preliminaries.

Let ℋ\mathcal{H} be the set of hospitals, 𝒮\mathcal{S} the set of medical services (e.g., Surgery, Radiology, Triage, Ward), and ℛ\mathcal{R} the set of resource types (e.g., IV Kits, Anesthetics, PPE kits). Let 𝒫\mathcal{P} be the set of patients. Each patient p∈𝒫p\in\mathcal{P} has an arrival time Tpa​r​rT_{p}^{arr} and a pathway sequence of KpK_{p} steps. Each step k∈{1,…,Kp}k\in\{1,\dots,K_{p}\} requires a specific service sp,k∈𝒮s_{p,k}\in\mathcal{S} and has a duration δp,k\delta_{p,k}. Resources are consumed according to a map C:𝒮×ℛ→ℕC:\mathcal{S}\times\mathcal{R}\to\mathbb{N}, where C⁡(s,r)C(s,r) is the quantity of resource rr required per scheduled patient step of service ss (if inventory is insufficient, the step can still be scheduled and a resource failure is recorded).

Agents, variables, and actions.

This environment involves two kinds of agents.

  • •

    Departmental agents. Denoted by 𝒜d​e​p​t={ah,s∣h∈ℋ,s∈𝒮}\mathcal{A}_{dept}=\{a_{h,s}\mid h\in\mathcal{H},s\in\mathcal{S}\}, the agent ah,s∈𝒜d​e​p​ta_{h,s}\in\mathcal{A}_{dept} is responsible for managing the service queue for service ss at hospital hh subject to capacity constraints.

  • •

    Resource provisioner agent. A single agent aprova_{\text{prov}} facilitating inventory transfers, holding its own stockpile of resources (and it may send to, or receive from, hospitals).

For each patient pp and step kk, the decision to schedule step kk is represented by selecting a start time

τp,k∈{t∈ℕ∣0≤t<T}∪{ϕ},\tau_{p,k}\in\{t\in\mathbb{N}\mid 0\leq t<T\}\cup\{\phi\},

with horizon T=168T=168 (the number of hours in a week), subject to precedence constraints (only the next unscheduled step is eligible) and to inter-hospital transfer time penalties between consecutive steps:

τp,k≥τp,k−1+δp,k−1+4⋅𝟏[hospital(p,k−1)≠hospital(p,k)](k>1).\tau_{p,k}\geq\tau_{p,k-1}+\delta_{p,k-1}+4\cdot\mathbf{1}[\text{hospital}(p,k-1)\neq\text{hospital}(p,k)]\quad(k>1).

τp,k=ϕ\tau_{p,k}=\phi implies that the step was unscheduled.

Simultaneously, agents may select transfer variables zr,i,j∈ℕz_{r,i,j}\in\mathbb{N} representing the amount of resource rr moved from inventory holder ii to inventory holder jj, capped by available sender inventory.

Local reward functions.

The objective function encourages patient throughput, successful completion of all pathways, adherence to resource constraints (via penalties for failures), and separate incentives for holding inventory versus executing transfers.

(1) Patient Flow and Completion (one function per patient):

fp​(𝝉p)={1000−(maxk⁡(τp,k+δp,k)−Tpa​r​r)if all steps scheduled,−500⋅(Kp−Nscheduled steps of p)otherwise.f_{p}(\bm{\tau}_{p})=\begin{cases}1000-\big(\max_{k}(\tau_{p,k}+\delta_{p,k})-T_{p}^{arr}\big)&\text{if all steps scheduled,}\\ -500\cdot\big(K_{p}-N_{\text{scheduled steps of $p$}}\big)&\text{otherwise.}\end{cases}

Where Nscheduled steps of p≜|{τp,k∣τp,k≠ϕ}|N_{\text{scheduled steps of $p$}}\triangleq|\{\tau_{p,k}\mid\tau_{p,k}\neq\phi\}| is the number of steps in pp’s pathway that were scheduled successfully.

The scope is the set of all start times for patient pp: scp⁡(fp)={τp,1,…,τp,Kp}\mathrm{scp}(f_{p})=\{\tau_{p,1},\dots,\tau_{p,K_{p}}\}.

(2) Resource Failures (global penalty, attributed to the failing agent at execution time):

g(𝝉)=−300⋅F,g(\bm{\tau})=-300\cdot F,

where FF is the total number of recorded resource failures (i.e., not possessing adequate resources for a scheduled step τp,k\tau_{p,k}, counted per failure event).

(3) Holding costs (non-hoarding) (hospital inventory only):

H(𝐈)=−∑h∈ℋ,r∈ℛ(10⋅Ih,rfinal),H(\mathbf{I})=-\sum_{h\in\mathcal{H},r\in\mathcal{R}}(10\cdot I_{h,r}^{\text{final}}),

where Ih,rfinalI_{h,r}^{\text{final}} is the unused inventory of resource rr remaining at the end of the episode at hospital hh (excluding the provisioner’s inventory).

(4) Transfer rewards (hospital-to-hospital transfers only, credited to the individual sender agent per resource unit sent):

L(𝐳)=∑r,i,j:i,j∈ℋ,i≠j(15⋅zr,i,j).L(\mathbf{z})=\sum_{r,i,j:\ i,j\in\mathcal{H},\,i\neq j}(15\cdot z_{r,i,j}).

Joint reward (the DCOP objective).

The global DCOP objective is to maximize the aggregate reward:

R⁡(𝝉,𝐳)=∑p∈𝒫fp​(𝝉p)+g⁡(𝝉)+H⁡(𝐈)+L⁡(𝐳).R(\bm{\tau},\mathbf{z})=\sum_{p\in\mathcal{P}}f_{p}(\bm{\tau}_{p})\;+\;g(\bm{\tau})\;+\;H(\mathbf{I})\;+\;L(\mathbf{z}).

B.2 Jira Ticket Allocation Environment

Large codebases rely on issue tracking to coordinate task allocation across engineers. In Jira, work items are tickets assigned based on expertise and availability. Agents act on behalf of specialized engineers (e.g., machine learning, refactoring) and coordinate using local/private information (e.g., workload, expertise, human-overseer availability) to propose effective, non-conflicting ticket assignments.

We model a one-shot Jira-style microtask allocation problem as implemented in Terrarium’s JiraTicketEnvironment. Agents may communicate during planning, but each agent ultimately commits at most one task choice (or skips) during execution. Unlike a multi-sprint scheduler, this environment has no explicit due sprints and no precedence constraints; all coupling is through soft penalties for collisions (duplicate task claims).

Preliminaries.

Let 𝒰\mathcal{U} be the set of agents (engineers) and 𝒯\mathcal{T} the set of available tasks (microtasks). Each task t∈𝒯t\in\mathcal{T} has public metadata: (i) skill tags GtG_{t} (typically 1–2 tags), (ii) effort et>0e_{t}>0, and (iii) a priority label pt∈{low,medium,high,critical}p_{t}\in\{\text{low},\text{medium},\text{high},\text{critical}\}. Each agent u∈𝒰u\in\mathcal{U} has private attributes: availability au>0a_{u}>0 and skills su,g∈[0,1]s_{u,g}\in[0,1] for tags gg (unlisted tags are treated as skill 00).

Actions (execution-phase decision variables).

Each agent chooses exactly one value

zu∈𝒯∪{⊥},z_{u}\in\mathcal{T}\cup\{\bot\},

where zu=tz_{u}=t means agent uu claims task tt, and zu=⊥z_{u}=\bot means skip. The joint action is 𝐳=(zu)u∈𝒰\mathbf{z}=(z_{u})_{u\in\mathcal{U}}.

Private cost model (skills + load).

For an agent–task pair (u,t)(u,t), define the tag-match score

mu,t={1|Gt|​∑g∈Gtsu,g|Gt|>0,0|Gt|=0.m_{u,t}\;=\;\begin{cases}\frac{1}{|G_{t}|}\sum_{g\in G_{t}}s_{u,g}&|G_{t}|>0,\\ 0&|G_{t}|=0.\end{cases}

Given hyperparameters ε>0\varepsilon>0 (skill_eps) and λ≥0\lambda\geq 0 (cost_weights.load), the private cost is

cu,t=etmax⁡(ε,mu,t+ε)⏟skill-adjusted effort+λ⋅max⁡(0,et−au)⏟overload penalty.c_{u,t}\;=\;\underbrace{\frac{e_{t}}{\max(\varepsilon,\,m_{u,t}+\varepsilon)}}_{\text{skill-adjusted effort}}\;+\;\underbrace{\lambda\cdot\max(0,\,e_{t}-a_{u})}_{\text{overload penalty}}.

Costs are precomputed and treated as private to each agent.

Joint score (single scalar objective).

Let w⁡(pt)w(p_{t}) map priority labels to weights: w⁡(low)=0.25w(\text{low})=0.25, w⁡(medium)=0.5w(\text{medium})=0.5, w⁡(high)=0.75w(\text{high})=0.75, w⁡(critical)=1.0w(\text{critical})=1.0. Define:

tasks_done(𝐳)=∑u∈𝒰𝟏[zu≠⊥],priority_sum(𝐳)=∑u∈𝒰𝟏[zu≠⊥]⋅w(pzu),\mathrm{tasks\_done}(\mathbf{z})=\sum_{u\in\mathcal{U}}\mathbf{1}[z_{u}\neq\bot],\qquad\mathrm{priority\_sum}(\mathbf{z})=\sum_{u\in\mathcal{U}}\mathbf{1}[z_{u}\neq\bot]\cdot w(p_{z_{u}}),
total_cost(𝐳)=∑u∈𝒰𝟏[zu≠⊥]⋅cu,zu.\mathrm{total\_cost}(\mathbf{z})=\sum_{u\in\mathcal{U}}\mathbf{1}[z_{u}\neq\bot]\cdot c_{u,z_{u}}.

To softly enforce that each task is claimed by at most one agent, let nt​(𝐳)=|{u∈𝒰:zu=t}|n_{t}(\mathbf{z})=\left|\{u\in\mathcal{U}:z_{u}=t\}\right| and define the collision count

violations⁡(𝐳)=∑t∈𝒯max⁡(0,nt​(𝐳)−1).\mathrm{violations}(\mathbf{z})=\sum_{t\in\mathcal{T}}\max(0,\,n_{t}(\mathbf{z})-1).

With weights BdoneB_{\text{done}} (tasks_done_bonus), BprioB_{\text{prio}} (priority_bonus), and PviolP_{\text{viol}} (violation_penalty), the environment score is

score⁡(𝐳)=Bdone⋅tasks​_​done​(𝐳)+Bprio⋅priority​_​sum​(𝐳)−total​_​cost​(𝐳)−Pviol⋅violations⁡(𝐳).\mathrm{score}(\mathbf{z})=B_{\text{done}}\cdot\mathrm{tasks\_done}(\mathbf{z})+B_{\text{prio}}\cdot\mathrm{priority\_sum}(\mathbf{z})-\mathrm{total\_cost}(\mathbf{z})-P_{\text{viol}}\cdot\mathrm{violations}(\mathbf{z}).

Larger BdoneB_{\text{done}} makes the objective approximately lexicographic: prioritize completing more tasks, then higher priority, then lower cost, while discouraging collisions via PviolP_{\text{viol}}.

Optimization view.

The induced optimization problem is

𝐳⋆∈arg⁡max𝐳∈(𝒯∪{⊥})|𝒰|⁡score⁡(𝐳).\mathbf{z}^{\star}\in\arg\max_{\mathbf{z}\in(\mathcal{T}\cup\{\bot\})^{|\mathcal{U}|}}\mathrm{score}(\mathbf{z}).

B.3 Meeting Scheduling Environment

Meeting Scheduling. Meeting scheduling optimizes attendance among agents with temporal and physical constraints, some of which may be private (e.g., a doctor’s appointment or tennis match). Agents coordinate to assign meetings to discrete time slots through communication, aiming to maximize attendance. We use the Meeting environment from CoLLAB [25], a DCOP benchmark for cooperative multi-agent systems (MAS). We refer to CoLLAB [25] for further details on this environment.

Appendix C Worst-Case Degradation Under Collusion

Proposition C.1 (Tight worst-case degradation under collusion).

Let Ω≜∏j=1mDj\Omega\triangleq\prod_{j=1}^{m}D_{j} be the (finite) set of complete assignments and let Fn:Ω→ℝF_{n}:\Omega\to\mathbb{R} be the original DCOP objective to be maximized, with 𝐱⋆\bm{x}^{\star} as the optimal assignment. Let 𝐱~\tilde{\mathbf{x}} be a Δ\Delta-collusive assignment, we write Δ⁡(𝐱~)≜Fn​(𝐱n⋆)−Fn​(𝐱~)\Delta(\tilde{\mathbf{x}})\triangleq F_{n}(\mathbf{x}^{\star}_{n})-F_{n}(\tilde{\mathbf{x}}). Then:

  1. 1.

    (Upper bound) For all 𝒙~∈Ω\tilde{\bm{x}}\in\Omega,

    Δ⁡(𝒙~)≤max𝒙∈Ω⁡Fn​(𝒙)−min𝒙∈Ω⁡Fn​(𝒙).\Delta(\tilde{\bm{x}})\leq\max_{\bm{x}\in\Omega}F_{n}(\bm{x})-\min_{\bm{x}\in\Omega}F_{n}(\bm{x}).
  2. 2.

    (Achievability) Assume an λ\lambda-aligned collusive coalition SS with λ>0\lambda>0 has sufficient control to enforce the maximizer of its effective objective Fλ​(𝒙)=(1−λ)​Fn​(𝒙)+λ​Fc​(𝒙)F_{\lambda}(\bm{x})=(1-\lambda)F_{n}(\bm{x})+\lambda F_{c}(\bm{x}) (e.g., the coalition can modify all factors defining the global objective). Then there exists a collusion objective FcF_{c} such that any maximizer of FλF_{\lambda} attains the upper bound, i.e., Δ⁡(𝒙~)=max⁡Fc−min⁡Fc\Delta(\tilde{\bm{x}})=\max F_{c}-\min F_{c}.

Proposition C.1 calibrates the maximum auditable harm under our nominal objective: any collusive outcome induces degradation at most max⁡Fn−min⁡Fn\max F_{n}-\min F_{n}, and sufficiently strong hidden incentives together with sufficient coalition influence can attain this worst case; we therefore use the resulting span as the natural scale for our auditing metrics in the LLM agent setting.

Appendix D Additional Results

D.1 Increasing Aggressiveness of Coalition Objective

In Fig 11, we vary prompts from the baseline (λ=0\lambda=0) to prompts that explicitly incite manipulation to increase coalition reward (λ=1\lambda=1). We find that a simple prompt that prompts the coalition to optimize the sum of their coalitional rewards increases coalition advantage more than instructions that aggressively incite adversarial techniques (e.g., deception, manipulation). This suggests adversarial behavior may not be particularly beneficial to the coalition. This is further justified by the inverse association between the judge score and coalition advantage in Figure 4 across 19 out-of-the-box models.

D.2 Mass Network Influence Effects

We study a mass misinformation strategy in the Meeting environment where each adversarial agent injects a false claim (e.g., that some agent aia_{i} is unavailable all week due to a trip) into the communication channel, but each new adversary selects a different victim agent. We evaluate this strategy over six communication-network families: three deterministic topologies (complete, path, star) and three random graph models (Barabási-Albert, Watts-Strogatz, Erdös-Renyi). Across these networks, increasing the number of adversaries generally reduces cooperative performance, yet misinformation belief often remains low in complete and star graphs because short path lengths (maximum two hops) enable benign agents to cross-check claims via nearby neighbors and reject inconsistent information.

D.3 Qualitative Analysis On Persuasion Trajectories

D.4 Persuasion in the Hospital Environment

We study the three persuasion techniques (i) Helpful misdirection, (ii) Authority nudge, (iii) Reciprocity trade. This allows us to fix the topology (a complete topology) and vary the objective of the coalition. The three objectives studied are (i) covert coalition reward maximization, where λ≈0.5\lambda\approx 0.5 w.r.t. a hidden objective FCF_{\text{C}}; (ii) destructive coalition reward maximization (Des (MCR)), where λ=1\lambda=1 w.r.t. FCF_{\text{C}}; and (iii) destructive no-reward prioritization (Des (NRP)), where λ=1\lambda=1 w.r.t. FC′F_{\text{C}}^{\prime}. We evaluate this on GPT-4.1-mini, GPT-4o-mini, and Kimi-K2.

D.5 How Much Does Agent Communication Order Matter?

We verified that the unsuccessful collusion attempt by Kimi-K2-Instruct agents is not due to the environment configuration, but rather to the agents’ inability to coordinate collusion. We compare the coalition’s regret with coalition ordered regret where coalition members take the first action in the environment (See Fig 13 in Appendix). Coalition ordered regret is defined as the regret given the actions available after certain actions have been claimed by agents in the previous round.

We find that both under random ordering and when colluders are allowed to act first, the colluders do not see a significant reduction in regret or gain in advantage. This suggests that better actions were available to the agents in their turns, but they did not take them.

E.1 Metric Details

N.B.

The prompts provided above are the basic misalignment prompts provided to agents in persuasion experiments on the Hospital environment in Section 5.6. These state the strategy desiderata but do not specify recommended courses of action so as to not interfere with persuasion prompts.

However, for the misalignment experiments in Section 5.5, significantly more sophisticated versions of these prompts were used, which are deferred to the GitHub repository and not included verbatim in the appendix owing to their length. These prompts, provided in the code in the GitHub repository were produced after several rounds of iterative manual prompt tuning of the basic misalignment prompts, yielding additional sophisticated strategic details and instructions, some of which are specific to the environment and the role of the adversarial agent (viz., if it is a resource provisioner or a departmental agent).
